title: guard-main-checkout-bash.sh reads quotes inside a $(…) command substitution as closing the outer double quote, so a `>` inside a quoted curl body is taken for a redirect and a read-only command from the primary checkout is blocked
body:
Filing gate: ① a defect with a named location and a reproduction — `.claude/hooks/guard-main-checkout-bash.sh`, reproduced against `origin/main` `a43405d596`.
Reader: the `domain:skills` lane, which owns the guard hooks (the earlier defects in this hook, #10570 and #11131, carry `domain:skills`). The fix is a PR to the hook and its self-test. `.claude/**` is Tier S.
Dedupe (open AND closed), objectstack: "guard-main-checkout-bash hook false positive greater-than inside quoted string read as redirect" → 7 hits; "guard-main-checkout-bash command substitution nested double quotes blocks read-only command" → 7 hits. The two queries return the same family, none on this. The nearest ones are about other shapes: #10570 and #10720 (a `>` in a shell comment), #11131 (an unquoted backslash) and #11133 (a heredoc introducer in a comment).
reach: named producer. The os-dev session that built #24802 / PR #24811 was blocked running a read-only `curl` probe. In cloud sessions the harness resets the shell's cwd to the primary checkout after every call, so the hook judges every such command against the primary checkout.
type: Bug

## What happens

The hook's quote-aware passes treat a `"` inside a `$(…)` that is itself inside a double-quoted word as the END of the outer quote. In a real shell, a command substitution opens a new quoting context, so the inner quotes nest. The hook then sees the inner text as unquoted, finds the `>` in a JSON body, and reports a write into the primary checkout whose target is the rest of the word.

The header promises the opposite: the hook acts only on shapes it can read with confidence, and everything else fails open (header lines 35 and 44, the latter listing `$(…)` among the unresolvable shapes).

## Reproduction

`cwd` = the primary checkout. Each command is fed to the hook as `{"tool_input":{"command":…},"cwd":"/home/user/objectstack"}` on stdin. `bash -n` accepts all three commands, and none of them writes a file.

| command | hook exit | hook's `target:` |
|---|---|---|
| `echo "a $(curl -d "{\"c\":\"x > 1\"}" http://h)"` | 2 (blocked) | `1"` |
| `echo "a $(curl -d '{"c":"x > 1"}' http://h)"` | 2 (blocked) | `1}' http://h)` |
| `curl -s -d "{\"c\":\"x > 1\"}" http://h` (no substitution) | 0 | — |
| control: `echo hi > out.txt` | 2 (blocked, correctly) | `out.txt` |

The original blocked command was a multi-line probe loop of the form `echo "PUT $1 -> $(curl … -d "{…\"condition\":\"int(record.title) > 1\"…}" $B/meta/object/$1)"`. The hook printed `command: > 1\"` and `target: 1"`.

## Expected

A `>` inside quotes inside a `$(…)` is not a redirect. Either track a command substitution as its own quoting context in both quote-aware passes (segmentation and tokenisation must agree, the lesson of #11131), or treat any double-quoted word containing `$(` as unreadable and fail open, as the header says. Add both forms above to `guard-main-checkout-bash.selftest.sh`, and keep the real-redirect control blocked.

Workaround in use: move the request into a script file in the scratchpad and run that.
